entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To be completely fed up with someone or something and unwilling to accept it any longer.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech when your patience runs out: *I've had it with this printer!* It's almost always in the present perfect (*I've had it*, *She's had it with him*), often with *with* + noun; *I've had it up to here* is even stronger. About an object (*My old laptop has had it*), it means broken or worn out.
examples: That's the third time the neighbors' car alarm has gone off tonight; **I've had it**.
My mom **has had it with** my brother leaving dirty dishes in the sink.
After two years of delays, residents **have had it with** the construction on Main Street.

drill.sentence: That's it, {{I've had it}} with this phone; it's frozen three times today.
drill.hint: what you say when your patience has run out (a contraction + two words; not *I'm done* or *I'm fed up*)

entries.related: *be fed up with* — same meaning, neutral; *be sick of* — tired of something, casual; *the last straw* — the final annoyance that makes you lose patience.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To like something or someone so much that you always want more of it.
entries.usage: Casual and enthusiastic, common in speech, reviews and ads: *I can't get enough of this song.* It's negative in form (*can't* or *couldn't*) but strongly positive in meaning. It's used for food, music, shows and places, and also for people (*Fans can't get enough of her*).
entries.pattern: can't / couldn't get enough of + noun
examples: I've played this album every day for a month; I just **can't get enough of** it.
My dad **can't get enough of** true-crime podcasts; he listens to them in the car, at the gym, everywhere.
The kids **couldn't get enough of** the dolphins and wanted to stay at the aquarium all day.

drill.sentence: My mom {{can't get enough of}} her new grandson; she visits him every single day.
drill.hint: loves so much that she always wants more time with (four words, starting with a negative; not *is crazy about*)

entries.related: *be crazy about* — love something or someone, casual; *be hooked on* — be addicted to something; *have had enough of* — the opposite, be fed up with.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To be addicted to something, or to enjoy it so much that you can't stop doing, watching or using it.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech for harmless obsessions such as TV shows, games, coffee and hobbies: *I'm totally hooked on this series.* It can also describe real addiction to drugs, alcohol or gambling, so context decides. *Get hooked* describes the start (*I got hooked after one episode*); the preposition is *on*.
examples: I watched one episode on Friday, and now I'm completely **hooked**.
Our neighbor **got hooked on** pickleball after he retired, and now he plays every morning.
The documentary follows three teenagers who **got hooked on** painkillers after sports injuries.

drill.sentence: My sister tried yoga in January, and now she's {{hooked}}; she goes five days a week.
drill.hint: unable to stop now (one word; not *obsessed* or *addicted*)

entries.related: *addicted to* — the neutral or medical word; *obsessed with* — thinking about something all the time; *can't get enough of* — love something and want more.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To like something a lot, or to think it's very important and give it a lot of attention.
entries.usage: Casual and common in American speech, very often in the negative: *I'm not big on sweets*, *I'm not big on surprises.* Use *on* + noun or *-ing* (*She's big on recycling*, *He's not big on talking about his feelings*). The negative is a polite, low-key way to say you don't like something.
examples: Our new principal is really **big on** reading; every class has twenty minutes of silent reading a day.
I'm not **big on** horror movies, so you guys go without me.
My mom was always **big on** manners: no phones at the table, and always say thank you.

drill.sentence: Thanks, but I'm not really {{big on}} birthday parties; let's just get dinner.
drill.hint: liking something a lot (two words; not *into* or *a fan of*)

entries.related: *be into* — be interested in or enjoy, casual; *be a fan of* — like, neutral; *be a stickler for* — insist on rules or details.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To feel sad, low or slightly depressed, often without a big reason.
entries.usage: Common and gentle in everyday speech, often with *a little*, *a bit* or *kind of*: *I've been feeling kind of down lately.* It's softer than *depressed*, which can sound like a medical condition. Careful: on its own, *I'm down* in casual American speech usually means *count me in*.
entries.pattern: feel / be (a little) down; something gets someone down
examples: Kara's been **feeling down** since her dog died, so let's take her out to dinner.
I always **feel** a bit **down** in February, when it's dark by five.
If you're **feeling down** about the breakup, call me anytime; I mean it.

drill.sentence: Long, gray winters always leave me {{feeling down}}, so I try to get outside every day.
drill.hint: a bit sad (two words; not *… blue* or *… low*)

entries.related: *feel blue* — same, a bit old-fashioned; *get someone down* — make someone sad (*The rain gets me down*); *depressed* — stronger, can be a medical term.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: In a bad mood, easily annoyed and complaining, often for a short time, for example when tired or hungry.
entries.usage: Casual and fairly mild, often affectionate or self-mocking: *I'm grumpy before my coffee.* It suits short moods (*grumpy in the morning*) and also people with that personality (*a grumpy old man*). It's gentler than *angry* and less serious than *bitter*.
examples: Don't talk to Dad before he's had his coffee; he's always **grumpy** in the morning.
The cashier was a little **grumpy**, but honestly, I would be too after a ten-hour shift.
Our **grumpy** neighbor yells at anyone who parks in front of his house.

drill.sentence: Sorry I snapped at you; I didn't sleep much last night, and I'm a little {{grumpy}}.
drill.hint: in a bad mood and easily annoyed (one word; not *cranky*, *moody*, *grouchy* or *irritable*)

entries.related: *cranky* — very similar, especially US; *grouchy* — similar, often a bit more lasting; *moody* — with moods that change often.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Overexcited and too full of energy, unable to calm down or sit still.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech about kids, pets, and adults after too much caffeine or sugar: *The kids are so hyper today.* It's short for *hyperactive*, which sounds more medical. It describes restless physical energy; for being excited about an upcoming event, Americans say *hyped* or *pumped*.
examples: The kids had cake and soda at the party, and now they're bouncing off the walls; they're so **hyper**.
I can't drink coffee after noon; it makes me way too **hyper** to sleep.
Our puppy gets **hyper** every time someone rings the doorbell.

drill.sentence: Don't give him any more candy; he's already running in circles and way too {{hyper}}.
drill.hint: full of uncontrolled energy (one word; not *excited* or *wired*)

entries.related: *hyperactive* — the full, more medical word; *wired* — very alert and restless, often from caffeine; *bouncing off the walls* — idiom, extremely hyper.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To take or keep more than your fair share of something, so others can't use it.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, very common about shared things: *hog the bathroom*, *hog the remote*, *hog the covers*, *hog the conversation*. It usually takes *the* + a shared thing and often comes with *always* or *stop*. In US sports, *a ball hog* is a player who never passes.
examples: My brother **hogs** the bathroom every morning, so I'm always late for school.
Stop **hogging** the blanket; I'm freezing over here.
At the town meeting, one man **hogged** the microphone for twenty minutes.

drill.sentence: My roommate always {{hogs}} the TV, so I end up watching everything on my phone.
drill.hint: takes more than his fair share of (one word; not *monopolizes*)

entries.related: *monopolize* — formal, same idea; *a ball hog* — US, a player who won't pass the ball; *share* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To talk too proudly about yourself, your achievements or what you own, in a way that annoys others.
entries.usage: Casual and critical: *He's always bragging about his car.* Use *brag about* + noun or *-ing*, or *brag that* + clause. *Not to brag, but …* is a common joking opener before you do exactly that, and *bragging rights* means the right to boast after winning.
examples: My cousin keeps **bragging** about how much money he makes, and it's getting old.
Not to **brag**, but I made the best pie at the bake sale.
Our team won the softball game and has been **bragging** about it all week.

drill.sentence: He's nice, but he never stops {{bragging}} about how fast he can run a marathon.
drill.hint: talking too proudly (one word; not *boasting* or a neutral word like *talking*)

entries.related: *boast* — same meaning, a bit more formal; *show off* — try to impress people, often by actions; *humblebrag* — brag while pretending to complain or be modest.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To fail an exam, test or course; also, of a teacher, to give a student a failing grade.
entries.usage: Casual and mainly American, common among students and parents: *I flunked my driving test.* It takes a direct object (*flunk a test*, *flunk chemistry*), and *flunk out (of school)* means be forced to leave because of bad grades. A teacher can also flunk a student: *She flunked half the class.*
entries.pattern: flunk + a test / a class; flunk out (of school)
examples: I **flunked** my first driving test because I forgot to signal.
He partied too much his freshman year and almost **flunked out** of college.
My chemistry teacher **flunked** half the class on the midterm.

drill.sentence: If you don't start studying for your Spanish final, you're going to {{flunk}} it.
drill.hint: casual US verb for failing a test (not *fail* or *bomb*)

entries.related: *fail* — the neutral word; *bomb* — do very badly on a test, slang; *ace* — the opposite, do very well.

entries.label: interjection
entries.meaning: An exclamation that shows a strong feeling such as surprise, frustration, disappointment or admiration.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech, at the start of a sentence: *Man, that was close!* Everyone uses it, and it isn't addressed to a man; the tone shows the feeling. *Oh man* often shows disappointment (*Oh man, I forgot my wallet*).
examples: **Man**, that truck almost hit us!
Oh **man**, I left my lunch on the kitchen counter again.
**Man**, that kid can really dance!

drill.sentence: {{Man}}, I can't believe the game went into triple overtime!
drill.hint: a short exclamation of strong feeling (three letters; not *wow* or *boy*)

entries.related: *boy* — a similar exclamation, a bit old-fashioned; *dude* — similar, younger slang; *wow* — surprise or admiration only.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Very big, good or bad of its kind; it goes before a noun to make it stronger.
entries.usage: Casual and friendly, mostly American: *That was a heck of a game.* It can be positive or negative (*a heck of a job*, *a heck of a mess*), and the context shows which. *Heck* is a mild replacement for *hell*, so *a hell of a* is stronger and less polite.
examples: That was **a heck of a** storm last night; we lost power for six hours.
You did **a heck of a** job on the yard; it looks like a park.
It's **a heck of a** drive from Boston to Miami if you do it in one day.

drill.sentence: Twelve inches of snow in one night? That's {{a heck of a}} way to start the year.
drill.hint: a mild, emphatic way to stress the noun (four words; not *quite a* or the ruder version with *hell*)

entries.related: *a hell of a* — same, stronger and less polite; *quite a* — neutral (*quite a game*); *one heck of a* — even more emphatic.

entries.label: intensifier
entries.meaning: Very or extremely; an intensifier before adjectives and nouns, used as a milder replacement for a swear word.
entries.usage: Slang, common in casual American speech among adults and teens: *It's freaking cold.* It shows annoyance or strong emotion, and because it softens a vulgar word, most people accept it with friends; it's still too rough for work emails or formal settings. *Frickin'* is a similar form.
examples: It's **freaking** freezing out there; grab a heavier coat.
I've been on hold with the cable company for a **freaking** hour.
That concert was **freaking** amazing; I lost my voice from screaming.

drill.sentence: Who left the {{freaking}} door open? The cat got out again!
drill.hint: a softened swear word showing annoyance (an *-ing* slang word; not *fricking* or *frigging*)

entries.related: *frickin'* — similar; *darn* — a milder, more old-fashioned substitute; *really* / *so* — the neutral intensifiers.

entries.label: texting abbreviation
entries.meaning: Short for *to be honest*: it introduces an honest opinion, often one that is a little critical or surprising.
entries.usage: Mainly in texts, chats and social media, written *TBH* or *tbh*, at the start or end of the message. Some younger speakers also say it aloud as letters, which sounds playful. In a work email, write *honestly* or *to be honest* instead.
examples: My friend texted after the movie: "**TBH** I didn't love it, but the soundtrack was great."
My roommate texted, "**TBH** the new coffee place is overpriced. Let's go back to Joe's."
My cousin commented on my new profile picture: "Way better than the old one, **TBH**."

drill.sentence: I texted Mia, "{{TBH}} I'd rather skip the party and just stay in tonight."
drill.hint: texting abbreviation for being frank (three letters; not *IMO*)

entries.related: *IMO* — in my opinion; *honestly* — the spoken equivalent; *ngl* — *not gonna lie*, used the same way in texts.

entries.label: texting abbreviation
entries.meaning: Short for *in my opinion*: it marks a statement as your personal view.
entries.usage: Used in texts, chats, comments and online forums, usually at the start or end of a sentence. *IMHO* (*in my humble opinion*) is a variant that's often ironic, since the opinion is rarely humble. It's too casual for formal emails; in speech, people say *I think* or *if you ask me*.
examples: In the group chat I wrote, "The sequel was way better than the original **IMO**."
My sister texted, "**IMO** you should take the Denver job. The other commute is way too long."
One comment under the pizza recipe said, "**IMO** pineapple on pizza is totally fine."

drill.sentence: I posted in the neighborhood group, "{{IMO}} the new coffee place is overrated; the diner's pancakes are better."
drill.hint: texting abbreviation that marks a personal view (three letters; not *TBH*)

entries.related: *IMHO* — same, often ironic; *TBH* — to be honest; *if you ask me* — the spoken equivalent.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Used to insist that what you're saying is really true, or that you will really do something.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech to stress that something is true (*I swear I locked the door*) or to promise (*I swear I'll pay you back*). It also introduces a frustrated threat or an exaggeration: *I swear, if he's late one more time …* In formal settings, say *I promise* or *I assure you*.
examples: I didn't eat the last cookie, **I swear**!
**I swear** I'll pay you back on Friday.
**I swear**, our cat understands every word we say.

drill.sentence: {{I swear}} I saw a bear in the backyard last night, but nobody believes me.
drill.hint: insisting it's true (two words; not *I promise* or *honestly*)

entries.related: *I promise* — neutral; *I'm not kidding* — stresses that you're serious; *swear* — also means use bad language.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To stop for a short rest, especially during physical effort or a stressful task.
entries.usage: Casual and common in sports, at work and in everyday life: *Let's take a breather.* It means a brief pause to recover, not a long break or a nap. It's fine in a relaxed meeting (*Why don't we take a five-minute breather?*); in formal writing, *a short break* fits better.
examples: We'd been hiking uphill for two hours, so we sat down on a rock to **take a breather**.
This meeting's been going for ninety minutes; can we **take a breather**?
Between the twins and his new job, Dan hasn't had a chance to **take a breather** in months.

drill.sentence: We've been cleaning out the garage all morning; let's {{take a breather}} and grab some lemonade.
drill.hint: stop and rest for a minute (three words; not ending in *break* or *rest*)

entries.related: *take five* — take a short break, casual; *catch your breath* — recover after physical effort; *take a break* — the neutral version.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Time you spend alone doing what you enjoy, free from work, family and other people's needs.
entries.usage: Casual and common in talk about busy lives, parenting and self-care: *I need some me time.* It's uncountable: *some me time*, *a little me time*, not *a me time*. It can sound like a magazine phrase, but most people use it without irony.
examples: After a week of looking after three kids on my own, I really need some **me time**.
Sunday mornings are my **me time**: coffee, a book, and no phone.
Her husband takes the kids to the park every Saturday so she can get some **me time**.

drill.sentence: I love my family, but a long bath with the door locked is my favorite kind of {{me time}}.
drill.hint: hours just for yourself (two words; not *alone* + noun)

entries.related: *alone time* — similar, focused on being alone; *self-care* — looking after your own health and mood; *downtime* — time to rest after work.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who hates spending money, even when it would be normal or fair to spend it.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, but often teasing: *Don't be such a cheapskate.* It's about people who avoid paying their share or always buy the cheapest of everything. The adjective *cheap* about a person means the same (*He's so cheap*), while *frugal* and *thrifty* are positive.
examples: My brother-in-law is such a **cheapskate** that he reuses tea bags three times.
Don't be a **cheapskate**; leave a real tip.
I'm not a **cheapskate**; I just don't see the point of a hundred-dollar haircut.

drill.sentence: He never buys a round of drinks and always "forgets" his wallet; what a {{cheapskate}}.
drill.hint: someone who won't spend money (one word; not *miser* or *tightwad*)

entries.related: *cheap* — the adjective (*He's so cheap*); *a tightwad* — same meaning, US; *frugal* — careful with money, positive.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very popular or widely discussed online right now, often listed by a social media site as a top topic.
entries.usage: Common in casual talk, news and marketing: *It's trending on TikTok.* Usually after *be* or *start*, often with *on* + platform, and also before a noun (*trending topics*). It describes popularity right now, not a long-term change, which is *a trend*.
examples: Your sister's dance video is **trending**; it has two million views since last night.
The hashtag started **trending** within an hour of the earthquake.
A local bakery's giant croissant was **trending** all weekend, and now there's a line around the block.

drill.sentence: After a famous singer posted a photo from our town's diner, the place was {{trending}} on social media for days.
drill.hint: being discussed by everyone online (one word; not *viral* or *popular*)

entries.related: *go viral* — spread very fast online; *buzzworthy* — getting a lot of attention; *a trend* — a general change over time.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A time, usually in the late afternoon or early evening, when a bar or restaurant sells drinks and snacks at lower prices.
entries.usage: A big part of American work culture: coworkers *go to happy hour* or *grab a drink at happy hour* after work, usually without an article. It also means the social event itself (*team happy hour on Thursday*), even when there are no discounts. It's neutral and fine in work emails.
examples: Tacos are two dollars during **happy hour**, from four to six.
A few of us are going to **happy hour** after work; want to come?
My parents still meet the neighbors for **happy hour** on the porch every Friday.

drill.sentence: Let's get to the bar before six so we can still order the cheap drinks at {{happy hour}}.
drill.hint: the bar's early-evening discount period (two words)

entries.related: *after-work drinks* — the neutral phrase; *a drink special* — a discounted drink; *a nightcap* — a last drink before bed.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A casual word for a psychiatrist, psychologist or therapist.
entries.usage: Casual and slightly joking; it comes from the older slang *headshrinker*. Many people use it lightly about their own therapy (*My shrink says I need boundaries*), but it can sound dismissive of mental-health care, so *therapist* is the safer word, especially with someone who is struggling.
examples: My **shrink** says I need to stop checking my work email at midnight.
He's been seeing a **shrink** since the divorce, and he seems much calmer.
You don't need a **shrink** to see that your brother is stressed about the wedding.

drill.sentence: She finally found a {{shrink}} she likes, and she says talking to someone every week really helps.
drill.hint: slang for a mental-health professional (one word; not *therapist* or *counselor*)

entries.related: *a therapist* — the neutral word; *a psychiatrist* — a medical doctor who can prescribe medication; *a counselor* — gives advice, often in schools or for specific problems.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A lazy person who avoids work or effort and does as little as possible.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, common at school and work: *He's such a slacker.* It's also a typical joke about yourself (*I've been a total slacker this week*). The phrasal verb is *slack off*: *Stop slacking off.*
examples: Kevin's a **slacker**; he takes two-hour lunches and leaves the hard jobs for everyone else.
I was a total **slacker** in high school and only started caring about grades in college.
I've been a **slacker** about going to the gym since the holidays.

drill.sentence: In every group project there's one {{slacker}} who does nothing and still gets the same grade.
drill.hint: a lazy person who avoids effort (one word; not *freeloader* or *loafer*)

entries.related: *slack off* — work less hard than you should; *a couch potato* — lazy at home, watching TV; *a go-getter* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Alcohol, or alcoholic drinks in general.
entries.usage: Casual and common in speech, headlines and jokes: *Who's bringing the booze?* It's uncountable and appears in compounds like *a booze cruise* (a party on a boat). It sounds a bit rough, so say *alcohol* or *drinks* in polite or formal settings.
examples: You bring the chips, and I'll bring the **booze**.
The stadium doesn't allow outside food or **booze**.
We spent more on **booze** than on food, and we ran out of chips by nine.

drill.sentence: We're having a backyard barbecue on Saturday; there'll be plenty of food, so just bring your own {{booze}}.
drill.hint: something to drink with alcohol in it (casual one-word noun; not *drinks*, *beer*, *wine* or *alcohol*)

entries.related: *alcohol* — neutral; *liquor* — US, strong drinks such as vodka and whiskey; *BYOB* — *bring your own bottle*, on invitations.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A customer who often goes to the same bar, café, restaurant or shop and is known there.
entries.usage: Common in everyday speech and fine in most contexts: *She's a regular at the coffee shop.* Usually *a regular at* + place; staff often treat regulars specially (*The usual?*). It also describes people who come often to a class or an event.
examples: The bartender started pouring my drink as soon as I walked in; I guess I'm **a regular** now.
The old men at the corner table are **regulars**; they've had breakfast here every morning for twenty years.
When the bookstore closed, the owner wrote a goodbye letter to all her **regulars**.

drill.sentence: He's been coming to this diner every Friday for ten years, so he's definitely {{a regular}}.
drill.hint: the word staff use for a frequent customer (two words; not *a local*)

entries.related: *a local* — someone who lives in the area; *the usual* — what a regular always orders; *a loyal customer* — business language.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something about a person or thing that makes you lose interest in them or stop liking them.
entries.usage: Common in casual talk, especially about dating (*Bad manners are a big turnoff*), but also about products, jobs and places. It's written *turnoff* or *turn-off*, and the verb is *turn someone off*. The opposite, *a turn-on*, is mostly sexual, so use it carefully.
examples: He was cute, but he was rude to the waiter, and that's a huge **turnoff** for me.
The apartment was nice, but the hour-long commute was a real **turnoff**.
Hidden fees at checkout are a big **turnoff** for most shoppers.

drill.sentence: I liked her at first, but the way she talked about her ex for an hour was a real {{turnoff}}.
drill.hint: something that kills your interest (one word; not *deal-breaker* or *red flag*)

entries.related: *a deal-breaker* — a problem big enough to end a relationship or deal; *a red flag* — a warning sign; *a turnoff* (road) — US, an exit from a highway.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A very sad or emotional movie, book, song or story that is meant to make people cry.
entries.usage: Casual and common in reviews and conversation: *That movie is a real tearjerker.* It's often neutral or positive, but it can suggest that the story tries too hard to make you cry. Also written *tear-jerker*.
examples: Bring tissues; that movie about the old dog is a total **tearjerker**.
The bride's dad gave a speech that was a total **tearjerker**; even the band was crying.
Every December the same holiday **tearjerker** is on TV, and every year my mom cries.

drill.sentence: I cried through the whole last chapter; that novel is a real {{tearjerker}}.
drill.hint: a story that makes you cry (one compound word; not *sob story*)

entries.related: *a sob story* — a sad personal story told to get sympathy; *heartbreaking* — very sad; *a feel-good movie* — the opposite, it makes you happy.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Tasting very good; delicious.
entries.usage: Very casual and a little childish: parents say it to kids, and adults use it playfully in texts and food posts (*This looks so yummy!*). In a restaurant review or at a formal dinner, *delicious* or *tasty* sound more adult. *Yum!* alone is the exclamation.
examples: Mmm, these pancakes are **yummy**; can I have another one?
Eat your carrots, sweetie; they're **yummy**.
Okay, that soup looks **yummy**; send me the recipe!

drill.sentence: The kids said the homemade pizza was super {{yummy}} and asked if we could make it again tomorrow.
drill.hint: the word kids use for food they love (not *tasty* or *good*)

entries.related: *delicious* — the neutral, adult word; *tasty* — good-tasting, casual; *yum* — an exclamation of pleasure about food.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Sleepy, weak and unable to think clearly, for example just after waking up, after an operation or when ill.
entries.usage: Common in everyday speech, often with *feel* or *wake up*: *I woke up groggy.* It describes a short-term state, often from bad sleep, jet lag, medication or anesthesia. It's neutral enough for a doctor's office or a work message (*I'm still a bit groggy from the flight*).
examples: I took some cold medicine last night and woke up totally **groggy**.
After the surgery, Dad was **groggy** for a few hours but recognized everyone.
That red-eye flight left me so **groggy** that I put salt in my coffee.

drill.sentence: I slept through three alarms and was still {{groggy}} when I got to work.
drill.hint: slow and foggy-headed after sleep (one word; not *sleepy*, *drowsy* or *tired*)

entries.related: *drowsy* — sleepy, often from medicine; *out of it* — not alert, casual; *wide awake* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A lazy, messy person who doesn't care about cleanliness or how they look.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, often said about roommates, partners and teenagers, or about yourself with humor: *I'm kind of a slob.* It's stronger than calling someone *messy*, and it covers both an untidy home and a sloppy appearance. Often with *total* or *such a*.
examples: My college roommate was a total **slob**: pizza boxes under the bed and clothes everywhere.
I'm a **slob** on weekends; I don't change out of my sweatpants until noon.
Don't show up to the interview looking like a **slob**; at least iron your shirt.

drill.sentence: He never washes a dish and leaves wet towels all over the floor; he's such a {{slob}}.
drill.hint: a lazy, messy person (one word; not *pig*)

entries.related: *messy* — untidy, milder; *a pig* — an insulting word for a messy or greedy person; *a neat freak* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To look around a place or through someone's private things secretly, trying to find out information.
entries.usage: Casual and critical: *Were you snooping through my phone?* Common patterns are *snoop around* (a place), *snoop through* or *snoop in* (things), and *snoop on* someone. A person who does this is *a snoop*, and the adjective is *snoopy*.
entries.pattern: snoop around (a place); snoop through / in something; snoop on someone
examples: I caught my roommate **snooping through** my mail while I was in the shower.
A man was **snooping around** the empty house next door, so I called the police.
Don't **snoop** in your sister's diary; it's private.

drill.sentence: Our new neighbor is always {{snooping around}} in our yard, pretending to look for his cat.
drill.hint: secretly looking for information (two words; not *poking …* or *nosing …*)

entries.related: *nosy* — too interested in other people's business; *pry* — try to find out private things, more formal; *spy on* — watch someone secretly.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A very kind, gentle, lovable person; also an affectionate way to address someone.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, about men and women alike: *Your grandma's a sweetheart.* As a form of address (*Thanks, sweetheart*), it's fine with your partner or children, but from a stranger, especially a man speaking to a woman at work, it can sound condescending.
examples: Your new neighbor is a total **sweetheart**; she brought us cookies on our first day.
Thanks for picking me up, **sweetheart**; I don't know what I'd do without you.
The big biker next door looks scary, but he's a real **sweetheart** once you get to know him.

drill.sentence: The mechanic fixed my flat tire and wouldn't take any money; what a {{sweetheart}}.
drill.hint: an especially kind, lovable person (one compound word; not *sweetie*, *angel* or *saint*)

entries.related: *sweetie* / *honey* — terms of address for loved ones; *an angel* — someone very kind or helpful; *a gem* — a wonderful person.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To insult or boast to an opponent, especially in sports or games, to provoke them or shake their confidence.
entries.usage: Common in American sports culture and among friends playing games: *They trash-talked each other all game.* The noun is usually written without a hyphen (*a lot of trash talk*). Outside games, *trash-talk someone* can also mean criticize them harshly.
examples: The two teams were **trash-talking** each other before the game even started.
My grandma **trash-talks** everyone at family Monopoly night, and she usually wins.
The two boxers **trash-talked** each other at the weigh-in, then hugged after the fight.

drill.sentence: We were playing pickup basketball, and the guys on the other team wouldn't stop {{trash-talking}} us.
drill.hint: provoking opponents with insults and boasts (hyphenated; not *taunting*)

entries.related: *smack talk* — same meaning, slang; *taunt* — tease or provoke, neutral; *trash someone* — US, criticize someone harshly.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone who enjoys being at home and prefers quiet evenings in to going out.
entries.usage: Casual and usually positive or neutral, often said about yourself: *I'm a total homebody.* Unlike *couch potato*, it doesn't suggest laziness, just a preference for home. British speakers more often say *a homebird*.
examples: I'm a **homebody**; my ideal Friday night is pizza, a movie and bed by ten.
My parents were always **homebodies**, so it's funny that they're now traveling around Europe.
Our cat is a real **homebody**; she runs back inside the minute we open the door.

drill.sentence: She'd rather stay in with a book than go to a club; she's always been a {{homebody}}.
drill.hint: someone who loves staying in (one word; not *introvert* or *recluse*)

entries.related: *a couch potato* — lazy, watches TV; *an introvert* — gets energy from being alone; *a party animal* — the opposite.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To understand the situation as a whole, without needing every detail explained.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, often at the end of a short list or description (*… you get the picture*) to avoid giving more details. As a question (*Get the picture?*) it can sound impatient, as if the listener should already understand. *I get the picture* politely tells someone they can stop explaining.
examples: The kitchen was flooded, the dog was barking and the baby was screaming; you **get the picture**.
She kept checking her watch until her guests finally **got the picture** and went home.
His teachers had warned him three times about being late, and he still didn't **get the picture**.

drill.sentence: You don't have to explain the rest of the story; I {{get the picture}}.
drill.hint: understand the overall situation (three words; not ending in *idea*, *gist* or *point*)

entries.related: *get the idea* — same, neutral; *get the hint* — understand an indirect message; *the big picture* — the overall situation.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A clumsy person who often drops things, trips or knocks things over.
entries.usage: Casual and usually affectionate or self-mocking: *I'm such a klutz.* It comes from Yiddish and is mainly American. The adjective is *klutzy*.
examples: I'm such a **klutz**; I tripped over my own feet walking into the restaurant.
Don't let Rob carry the wedding cake; he's a total **klutz**.
My daughter's a bit of a **klutz**, so we bought the toughest phone case we could find.

drill.sentence: I spilled coffee on my shirt, knocked over a lamp and dropped my phone, all before nine; I'm such a {{klutz}}.
drill.hint: a clumsy person (one word, from Yiddish; not *butterfingers*)

entries.related: *clumsy* — the neutral adjective; *butterfingers* — someone who drops things, often said as a joke; *all thumbs* — bad with your hands.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A parent who watches and controls their child's life too closely, even when the child is old enough to manage alone.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, common in talk about schools, colleges and parenting: *His mom is a total helicopter parent.* The image is a helicopter hovering over the child. Typical stories involve parents calling teachers about grades or doing their child's homework; the neutral adjective is *overprotective*.
examples: My mom was a **helicopter parent**; she called my college professors when I got a B.
Some **helicopter parents** follow their kids around the playground and catch them before every fall.
Try not to be a **helicopter parent**; let her walk to school with her friends.

drill.sentence: He's twenty-five, and his dad still calls his boss when he's unhappy with his schedule; talk about a {{helicopter parent}}.
drill.hint: an overprotective, controlling mom or dad (two words; not *tiger mom*)

entries.related: *overprotective* — the neutral adjective; *a tiger mom* — a strict mother who pushes her child to achieve; *a free-range parent* — gives children a lot of independence.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The people with more power and authority in an organization, such as senior managers or executives.
entries.usage: Casual, used at work about bosses you rarely see: *The higher-ups decided to close the office.* It's almost always plural with *the*, and it often sounds distant or a little resentful, as if decisions come from above. In formal writing, use *senior management* or *leadership*.
examples: Our manager likes the idea, but she has to run it by the **higher-ups** first.
The **higher-ups** at the hospital cut the nursing staff, and now everyone's working double shifts.
The store manager wanted to close for Thanksgiving, but the **higher-ups** at headquarters said no.

drill.sentence: We all want to work from home on Fridays, but the decision is up to {{the higher-ups}}.
drill.hint: senior managers, informally (hyphenated; not *the brass* or *the suits*)

entries.related: *top brass* — the most senior people, originally military; *the suits* — management, slightly mocking; *the powers that be* — the people in control, a bit ironic.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A short sleep, usually under thirty minutes, taken to feel more alert and energetic.
entries.usage: Casual and positive, common at work and among students and athletes: *I'm going to grab a quick power nap.* Use it with *take* or *grab*. The word *power* makes the nap sound productive rather than lazy.
examples: I grabbed a twenty-minute **power nap** in the car before my night shift.
My grandpa swears by a **power nap** after lunch; he says it's his secret to living to ninety.
Some companies now have quiet rooms where employees can take a **power nap**.

drill.sentence: I'm exhausted after the long drive, so I'm going to take a quick {{power nap}} before dinner.
drill.hint: a short, energizing sleep (two words; not *catnap*)

entries.related: *a catnap* — a short, light sleep; *a siesta* — an afternoon rest, from Spanish; *forty winks* — old-fashioned for a short sleep.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A shared meal where each guest brings a dish for everyone to eat.
entries.usage: Very common in American offices, schools, clubs and neighborhoods: *an office potluck*, *a potluck dinner*. Guests often sign up for what they'll bring, so that not everyone brings dessert. The older phrase *take potluck* means accept whatever food or option happens to be available.
examples: Our neighborhood has a **potluck** every July; everyone brings a dish and we eat in the park.
I'm making mac and cheese for the office **potluck** tomorrow.
Their wedding reception was a **potluck**, so the food was a mix of tamales, lasagna and five kinds of potato salad.

drill.sentence: For Friendsgiving this year, we're doing a {{potluck}}: I'll roast the turkey, and everyone else brings sides.
drill.hint: a meal where each guest brings food (one word; not *buffet*)

entries.related: *a cookout* — US, an outdoor meal with grilled food; *BYOB* — *bring your own bottle*; *a buffet* — a meal where people serve themselves.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Fake, not genuine; of a person, pretending to be something they are not or showing feelings they don't have.
entries.usage: Casual and critical, used for people (*He's so phony*), feelings (*a phony smile*) and things (*a phony ID*). It's also a noun: *He's a phony*, which is a fairly strong insult. *Phony* is the American spelling; British English writes *phoney*.
examples: Her laugh sounds so **phony**; I can tell she doesn't actually think he's funny.
Police arrested a man selling **phony** concert tickets outside the stadium.
He acts like everyone's best friend, but I think he's a total **phony**.

drill.sentence: The guy at the door said he was from the gas company, but his badge looked totally {{phony}}.
drill.hint: not real, made to fool people (one word, US; not *fake* or *bogus*)

entries.related: *fake* — the general word; *bogus* — fake or false, casual; *the real deal* — the opposite, genuine.

entries.label: interjection
entries.meaning: A mild, polite substitute for *damn*, used to show annoyance or disappointment, or to add emphasis.
entries.usage: Mild and a bit old-fashioned, common among people who avoid swearing and around children: *Darn it!* It also works as an adjective or adverb for emphasis (*the darn car*, *a darn good pie*). Because it sounds quaint, younger speakers sometimes use it with humor.
examples: **Darn** it, I left my reading glasses at the restaurant again.
The **darn** cat knocked my coffee off the table.
That was a **darn** good pie, Mrs. Miller.

drill.sentence: {{Darn}}, I just missed the bus, and the next one isn't for forty minutes.
drill.hint: a polite way to curse (one word; not *shoot*, *dang* or *rats*)

entries.related: *dang* — a similar mild substitute; *shoot* — a mild exclamation of annoyance; *damn* — the stronger original.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone who criticizes or mocks others, especially successful people, often out of envy rather than for good reasons.
entries.usage: Slang that spread from hip-hop and is now common online and in casual speech. It's used to dismiss criticism as jealousy, as in the saying *Haters gonna hate*. Calling a critic a hater can be a joke, but it can also be a way to ignore fair criticism.
examples: Ignore the **haters**; your channel's growing every week.
My brother's new car is great; don't be a **hater** just because yours is older.
Every successful restaurant gets a few **haters** who leave one-star reviews without ever eating there.

drill.sentence: You got the lead role in the play? Don't listen to the {{haters}}; they're just jealous.
drill.hint: people who criticize out of envy (slang; not *trolls* or *critics*)

entries.related: *a troll* — someone who posts provocative or insulting comments online; *a critic* — neutral; *a sore loser* — someone bitter about losing.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Expensive, elegant and elaborate, often more than necessary; *nothing fancy* means something simple.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech: *a fancy restaurant*, *a fancy hotel*, *Let's go somewhere fancy.* It can be admiring or slightly mocking (*Ooh, fancy!*), and *nothing fancy* is a modest way to describe something simple. Don't confuse it with the British verb *fancy* (= want, or be attracted to), which Americans rarely use.
examples: The hotel was so **fancy** that they had a guy whose only job was opening the door.
Dinner's at my place, but it's nothing **fancy**, just burgers on the grill.
Look at you in a suit and tie; where are you going, somewhere **fancy**?

drill.sentence: We don't need a {{fancy}} hotel; somewhere clean near the beach is fine.
drill.hint: elegant and pricey, more than needed (one word; not *luxury*, *upscale*, *posh* or *expensive*)

entries.related: *upscale* — US, expensive and high-quality, common in ads; *posh* — British-sounding, elegant and expensive; *swanky* — fancy, a bit showy.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Doing extremely well, especially having a run of successes in a game or activity.
entries.usage: Casual and enthusiastic, from sports, where a player who keeps scoring is *on fire*. It's common as praise (*You're on fire today!*) for any streak of good results, from card games to sales. The literal meaning is *burning*, so the context must make the sense clear.
examples: Our quarterback is **on fire** tonight; that's his fourth touchdown.
You've won three hands in a row; you're **on fire**!
The sales team has been **on fire** this quarter, beating every target.

drill.sentence: She hit three home runs in one game; she's totally {{on fire}} this season.
drill.hint: having a streak of success (two words; not *on a roll* or *killing it*)

entries.related: *on a roll* — having a series of successes; *killing it* — doing extremely well, slang; *in the zone* — fully focused and performing well.

entries.label: interjection
entries.meaning: An exclamation of surprise or amazement; also a way to tell someone to slow down, stop or calm down.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech and texts: *Whoa, that's huge!* In the *slow down* sense (*Whoa, whoa, let's not panic*) it's often repeated; it was originally a command to stop a horse. The standard spelling is *whoa*, though *woah* is common online.
examples: **Whoa**, look at the size of that pumpkin!
**Whoa**, slow down; you're going way too fast for this road.
**Whoa**, whoa, whoa, nobody said anything about moving to Canada.

drill.sentence: {{Whoa}}, did you see that lightning? It hit the tree across the street!
drill.hint: an exclamation of amazement (not *wow*, *man* or *dude*)

entries.related: *wow* — surprise or admiration, without the *slow down* meaning; *hold on* / *wait a minute* — ask someone to stop; *yikes* — surprise mixed with alarm.

entries.label: interjection
entries.meaning: A sound that shows disgust, annoyance or frustration.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech and especially in texts: *Ugh, Mondays.* It's often followed by a short complaint, and in writing people stretch it (*ughhh*) to show how annoyed they are. It's fine with friends but sounds childish or rude as a reply to a coworker's request.
examples: **Ugh**, there's a hair in my soup.
**Ugh**, I have to get up at five tomorrow for a flight.
"The game's canceled because of rain." "**Ugh**, seriously? I already bought snacks."

drill.sentence: {{Ugh}}, the dishwasher's leaking again, and I just mopped the floor.
drill.hint: a sound of frustration (three letters; not *gah*)

entries.related: *yuck* / *ew* — disgust only; *argh* — frustration or anger; *sigh* — written in texts to show tiredness or disappointment.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone who loves reading and spends a lot of time reading books.
entries.usage: Casual and usually affectionate, said about children and adults: *She was a real bookworm as a kid.* It's mostly positive, but among kids it can suggest someone who reads instead of socializing. Common with *real*, *total* or *such a*.
examples: My daughter's such a **bookworm** that she reads at the dinner table if we let her.
As a kid, I was a total **bookworm** and spent every summer at the public library.
The new café in the bookstore is perfect for **bookworms**: comfy chairs, good coffee and no music.

drill.sentence: He finished all seven Harry Potter books in two weeks; he's a real {{bookworm}}.
drill.hint: someone who loves reading (one word; not *reader* or *nerd*)

entries.related: *a book lover* — neutral; *a nerd* — studious or obsessive, more mixed; *a bibliophile* — formal, a lover or collector of books.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone who loves going to parties, usually staying late and drinking or dancing a lot.
entries.usage: Casual and usually humorous, often about college students or someone's wild past: *He was a party animal in college.* It can be admiring or mildly critical, depending on tone. In the negative it's a modest joke: *I'm not much of a party animal.*
examples: My uncle was a **party animal** in his twenties; now he's in bed by nine.
I'm not much of a **party animal**; I'd rather have three friends over for board games.
Their daughter turned into a **party animal** her first semester and nearly lost her scholarship.

drill.sentence: She's out dancing every Friday and Saturday until three a.m.; she's a real {{party animal}}.
drill.hint: someone who loves wild nights out (two words; not *night owl*)

entries.related: *a night owl* — someone who stays up late, not necessarily partying; *a social butterfly* — someone who loves meeting people; *a homebody* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone who is obsessed with keeping things clean, tidy and organized.
entries.usage: Casual and usually teasing, often used about yourself: *I'm a bit of a neat freak.* *Freak* here means a person obsessed with something, as in *a control freak* or *a health freak*. It becomes a mild criticism when the tidiness bothers other people.
examples: My roommate's a **neat freak**; she reorganizes the fridge every time I buy groceries.
I'm a bit of a **neat freak**, so I can't relax until the dishes are done.
Being a **neat freak** with three kids and two dogs is a losing battle.

drill.sentence: He vacuums twice a day and labels every shelf in the pantry; he's a total {{neat freak}}.
drill.hint: someone obsessed with tidiness (two words; not the phrase starting with *clean*)

entries.related: *a clean freak* — same meaning; *a control freak* — someone who must control everything; *a slob* — the opposite.
